Membranous Nephropathy

  • Dr. Mustafa Salahalden

Overview

  • Membranous nephropathy is the second most common cause of nephrotic syndrome in adults, FSGS being the most common
  • Most common in men older than 40 years, usually people of European origins

Etiology

  • Primary: Idiopathic (70% of cases)
  • Secondary
  • Systemic lupus erythematosus, lupus could lead to membranous or to lupus nephritis which is nephritic
  • Solid tumors: colon cancer, lung cancer, melanoma
  • Infectious: hep B, hep C, syphilis
  • Drugs: penicillamine, gold, NSAIDs

Pathogenesis

  • Primary is an autoimmune disease mediated by IgG antibody (autoantibodies) directed to the phospholipase A2 receptor (PLA2R) on the podocytes, this attack lead to thickening of glomerular basement membrane which will be obvious on light microscopy
  • Secondary due to direct injury to the glomerular basement membrane

Renal biopsy

  • Light microscopy: Shows thickened glomerular basement membrane and that is why it is called membranous
  • Immunofluorescence shows deposition of granular IgG/ C3
  • Electron microscopy: subepithelial deposits (spike and dome appearance

Presentation

  • Frothy urine
  • Pitting edema, worse in lower extremities,
  • Periorbital edema
  • Abdominal pain due to ascites, severe hypovolemia, peritonitis, pancreatitis, thrombosis, or steroid induced gastritis
  • Hypertension
  • Patients may develop white nails sometimes in bands (Muehrcke's lines) during relapses
  • Patients may develop xanthomas and xanthelasma because of hyperlipidemia

Diagnosis

  • Nephrotic range proteinuria, urine dipstick test 3+, 4+
  • 24 hours urine protein is > 3.5g
  • Urine protein creatinine ratio of more than 3
  • Comprehensive metabolic panel looking for Hypoalbuminemia: serum albumin < 3
  • Renal function test: BUN and creatinine looking for renal dysfunction
  • Serum electrolytes looking for calcium and other electrolytes changes because Total serum calcium and vitamin D decreased due to decrease protein bound calcium and decrease vitamin D binding proteins lost in urine respectively, ionized calcium is usually normal
  • Mild hyponatremia during relapses
  • Normal serum completements
  • PLA2R antibodies positive in 70- 80% of primary MN cases and these antibodies with the nephrotic syndrome presentation are enough for MN diagnosis (no need of biopsy
  • Hepatitis serology testing
  • Elevated hemoglobin and hematocrit levels and thrombocytosis are usually found during relapse as result of plasma volume contraction
  • Confirmatory test is renal biopsy

Prognosis

  • One third of the patients with idiopathic MN undergo spontaneous remission, one third remain in nephrotic state and one third develop progressive CKD

Progression to ESRD

  • 15% of patients with MN progress to ESRD in 5 years if untreated, 40% at 15 years
  • Risk factors for progression
  • Elderly patients
  • Male gender
  • > 8 g of proteinuria at presentation
  • Tubulointerstitial fibrosis on biopsy

Treatment

  • Supportive therapy
  • Strict blood pressure control < 130/80 mmHg using ACEs or ARBs
  • Hyperlipidemia treated with statins
  • Edema treated with sodium restriction and diuretics
  • Thrombophilia treated with anticoagulation
  • Infections treated with antibiotics
  • Primary MN: Patient treated if they have risk factor for progression or nephrotic syndrome that can’t be controlled by ACEs or other supportive therapies
  • Cyclophosphamide + prednisolone
  • Cyclosporine + low dose prednisolone for those who cannot tolerate the first option
  • Rituximab (superior to other options)
  • Secondary MN treated by treating the secondary cause
